# Protein-First and Peptide World Theories

## Core Idea

Protein-first theories propose that simple peptides acted as primitive catalysts before nucleic-acid heredity emerged.

## Historical Context

These models emerged in response to the catalytic limitations of purely nucleic-acid-first scenarios.

## Mechanistic Basis

Short peptides may have accelerated reactions, stabilized intermediates, and supported metal-assisted catalysis.

## What the Theory Explains Well

Protein-first theories are strongest for primitive catalysis.

## What Makes It Plausible

Amino acids form readily, and short peptides can form under prebiotic conditions.

## Key Experimental / Observational Support

Peptide formation and metal-binding catalysis provide limited but suggestive support.

## Major Gaps and Critiques

The major gap is heredity: peptide systems lack a strong mechanism for encoded information.

## Current Scientific Standing

Protein-first theories are generally treated as secondary catalytic models rather than complete origin theories.

| Dimension | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Strength | Primitive catalysis |
| Plausibility | Moderate |
| Main Gap | Heredity |
| Current Standing | Useful but limited |
